nodes.title: Integrated Math 3
nodes.description: Students develop a deep understanding of quadratic relationships, multiple solution methods, and extend solutions into the complex number system. Emphasis is placed on connecting algebraic procedures with graphical meaning.

nodes.title: Example 1 Graph a Quadratic Function by Using a Table

metadata.rawText: Graph f(x) = x^2 + 2x - 3. State the domain and range.
metadata.demonstratedCapability: Graph a quadratic function by using a table and state its domain and range.

nodes.title: Example 2 Compare Quadratic Functions

metadata.rawText: Compare the graph of f(x) to a quadratic function g(x) with a y-intercept of -1 and a vertex at (1, 2). Which function has a greater maximum?

nodes.title: Example 3 Use Quadratic Functions

metadata.rawText: SKIING A ski resort has extended hours on one holiday weekend per year. Last year, the resort sold 680 ski passes at $120 per holiday weekend pass. This year, the resort is considering a price increase. They estimate that for each $5 increase, they will sell 20 fewer holiday weekend passes. Part A How much should they charge in order to maximize profit? Part B Find the domain and range in the context of the situation.
metadata.demonstratedCapability: Model profit with a quadratic function, find its maximum, and interpret contextual domain and range.

nodes.title: Example 4 Find Average Rate of Change from an Equation

metadata.rawText: Determine the average rate of change of f(x) = -x^2 + 2x - 1 over the interval [-4, 4].
metadata.demonstratedCapability: Calculate average rate of change from an equation over an interval.

metadata.rawText: Determine the average rate of change of f(x) over the interval [-3, 3].
metadata.demonstratedCapability: Calculate average rate of change from table values over an interval.

nodes.title: Example 6 Find Average Rate of Change from a Graph

metadata.rawText: Part A Use the graph to estimate the average rate of change of spending on sports footwear from 2005 to 2015. Then check your results algebraically.
metadata.demonstratedCapability: Estimate average rate of change from a graph and check the result algebraically.

nodes.title: Example 1: One Real Solution

metadata.rawText: Example 1: One Real Solution. Solve 10 - x^2 = 4x + 14 by graphing. Rearrange terms so that one side of the equation is 0. 0 = x^2 + 4x + 4. Find the axis of symmetry. x = -b/(2a) = -4/(2(1)) or -2. Make a table of values, plot the points, and connect them with a curve. The zero of the function is -2. Therefore, the solution of the equation is -2 or {x | x = -2}.

nodes.title: Example 2: Two Real Solutions

metadata.rawText: Example 2: Two Real Solutions. Use a quadratic equation to find two real numbers with a sum of 24 and a product of 143. Let x represent one of the numbers. Then 24 - x will represent the other number. So x(24 - x) = 143. Solve the equation for 0, find the axis of symmetry, and make a table of values and graph the function. The zeros of the function are 11 and 13. x = 11 or x = 13, so 24 - x = 13 or 24 - x = 11. Thus, the two numbers with a sum of 24 and a product of 143 are 11 and 13.

nodes.title: Example 3: Estimate Roots

metadata.rawText: Example 3: Estimate Roots. Solve -x^2 + 3x + 7 = 0 by graphing. If the exact roots cannot be found, state the consecutive integers between which the roots are located. Make a table of values, plot the points, and connect them with a curve. The x-intercepts of the graph indicate that one solution is between -2 and -1, and the other solution is between 4 and 5.

nodes.title: Example 4: Solve by Using a Table

metadata.rawText: Example 4: Solve by Using a Table. Use a table to solve -x^2 + 5x - 1 = 0. Enter -x^2 + 5x - 1 in the Y= list and use the TABLE window to find where the sign of Y1 changes. The sign changes between x = 0 and x = 1. Use TBLSET to change delta Tbl to 0.1 and repeat for 0.01 and 0.001. One zero is located at approximately x = 0.209. The zeros of the function are at approximately 0.209 and 4.791, so the solutions to the equation are approximately 0.209 and 4.791.

nodes.title: Example 5: Solve by Using a Calculator

metadata.rawText: Example 5: Solve by Using a Calculator. A kicker punts a football. The height of the ball after t seconds is given by h(t) = -16t^2 + 50t + h0, where h0 is the initial height. If the ball is 1.5 feet above the ground when the punter’s foot meets the ball, how long will it take the ball to hit the ground? We know that h0 is the initial height, so h0 = 1.5. We need to find t when h(t) is 0. Use a graphing calculator to graph the related function h(t) = -16t^2 + 50t + 1.5. Use the zero feature to find the positive zero. The zero is approximately 3.15. Thus, the ball hit the ground approximately 3.15 seconds after it was punted.

nodes.title: Example 1: Factor by Using the Distributive Property

metadata.rawText: PDF page 27, Example 1: Factor by Using the Distributive Property. Prompt: Solve 12x^2 - 2x = x by factoring. Check your solution. Solution: 12x^2 - 3x = 0; 3x(4x) - 3x(1) = 0; 3x(4x - 1) = 0; 3x = 0 or 4x - 1 = 0; x = 0 or x = 1/4. Capability: Factor the GCF and apply the Zero Product Property.

nodes.title: Example 2: Factor a Trinomial

metadata.rawText: PDF page 28, Example 2: Factor a Trinomial. Prompt: Solve x^2 - 6x - 9 = 18 by factoring. Check your solution. Solution: x^2 - 6x - 27 = 0; (x + 3)(x - 9) = 0; x + 3 = 0 or x - 9 = 0; x = -3 or x = 9. Capability: Factor a monic trinomial and apply the Zero Product Property.

nodes.title: Example 3: Solve an Equation by Factoring

metadata.rawText: PDF page 28, Apply Example 3: Solve an Equation by Factoring. Prompt: ACCELERATION The equation d = vt + 1/2 at^2 represents the displacement d of a car traveling at an initial velocity v where the acceleration a is constant over a given time t. Find how long it takes a car to accelerate from 30 mph to 45 mph if the car moved 605 feet and accelerated slowly at a rate of 2 feet per second squared. Solution: Convert 30 mph to 44 fps; 605 = 44t + t^2; t^2 + 44t - 605 = 0; (t + 55)(t - 11) = 0; t = -55 or t = 11; t = 11 s because time cannot be negative. Capability: Apply factoring to a contextual quadratic and select the viable solution.

nodes.title: Example 4: Factor a Trinomial Where a is Not 1

metadata.rawText: PDF page 29, Example 4: Factor a Trinomial Where a is Not 1. Prompt: Solve 3x^2 + 5x + 15 = 17 by factoring. Check your solution. Solution: 3x^2 + 5x - 2 = 0; (3x - 1)(x + 2) = 0; 3x - 1 = 0 or x + 2 = 0; x = 1/3 or x = -2. Capability: Factor a trinomial with a leading coefficient other than 1 and apply the Zero Product Property.

nodes.title: Example 5: Factor a Difference of Squares

metadata.rawText: PDF page 30, Example 5: Factor a Difference of Squares. Prompt: Solve 81 = x^2 by factoring. Check your solution. Solution: 81 - x^2 = 0; 9^2 - x^2 = 0; (9 + x)(9 - x) = 0; x = -9 or x = 9. Capability: Recognize a difference of squares and apply the Zero Product Property.

nodes.title: Example 6: Factor a Perfect Square Trinomial

metadata.rawText: PDF page 30, Example 6: Factor a Perfect Square Trinomial. Prompt: Solve 16y^2 - 22y + 23 = 26y - 13 by factoring. Check your solution. Solution: 16y^2 - 48y + 36 = 0; (4y)^2 + 2(4y)(-6) + (-6)^2 = 0; (4y - 6)^2 = 0; y = 3/2. Capability: Recognize a perfect square trinomial and solve by factoring.

nodes.title: Example 7: Complex Solutions

metadata.rawText: PDF page 30, Example 7: Complex Solutions. Prompt: Solve x^2 = -144 by factoring. Check your solution. Solution: x^2 + 144 = 0; x^2 - (-144) = 0; x^2 - (12i)^2 = 0; (x + 12i)(x - 12i) = 0; x = -12i or x = 12i. Capability: Factor a difference of squares over the complex numbers and apply the Zero Product Property.

nodes.title: Example 1: Solve a Quadratic Equation with Rational Roots

metadata.rawText: PDF page 33. Prompt: Solve x² − 4x + 4 = 25 by using the Square Root Property. Demonstrated capability: Use the Square Root Property to solve a quadratic equation with rational roots. Solution: (x − 2)² = 25, x − 2 = ±5, so x = 7 or x = −3.

nodes.title: Example 2: Solve a Quadratic Equation with Irrational Roots

metadata.rawText: PDF page 34. Prompt: Solve x² + 24x + 144 = 192 by using the Square Root Property. Demonstrated capability: Use the Square Root Property to solve a quadratic equation with irrational roots. Solution: (x + 12)² = 192, x = −12 ± 8√3, approximately 1.86 or −25.86.

nodes.title: Example 3: Solve a Quadratic Equation with Complex Solutions

metadata.rawText: PDF page 34. Prompt: Solve 2x² − 92x + 1058 = −72 by using the Square Root Property. Demonstrated capability: Use the Square Root Property to solve a quadratic equation with complex solutions. Solution: (x − 23)² = −36, x = 23 ± 6i.

nodes.title: Example 4: Complete the Square

metadata.rawText: PDF page 35. Prompt: Find the value of c that makes x² − 7x + c a perfect square. Then write the expression as a perfect square trinomial. Demonstrated capability: Find and use one-half of b squared to write a perfect square trinomial. Solution: half of −7 is −3.5; c = 12.25; x² − 7x + 12.25 = (x − 3.5)².

nodes.title: Example 5: Solve by Completing the Square

metadata.rawText: PDF page 35. Prompt: Solve x² + 18x − 4 = 0 by completing the square. Demonstrated capability: Solve a quadratic equation by completing the square and applying the Square Root Property. Solution: x² + 18x = 4; add 81; (x + 9)² = 85; x = −9 ± √85, approximately 0.22 or −18.22.

nodes.title: Example 7: Solve When a Is Not 1

metadata.rawText: PDF page 36. Prompt: Solve 4x² − 12x − 27 = 0 by completing the square. Demonstrated capability: Solve a quadratic equation by first making the coefficient of x² equal to 1. Solution: divide by 4; (x − 3/2)² = 9; x = 9/2 or −3/2.

nodes.title: Example 8: Solve Equations with Imaginary Solutions

metadata.rawText: PDF page 36. Prompt: Solve 3x² − 72x + 465 = 0 by completing the square. Demonstrated capability: Solve a quadratic equation with imaginary solutions by completing the square. Solution: divide by 3; (x − 12)² = −11; x = 12 ± i√11.

nodes.title: Example 9: Write Functions in Vertex Form

metadata.rawText: PDF page 37. Prompt: Write y = −x² − 12x − 9 in vertex form. Demonstrated capability: Rewrite a quadratic function in vertex form by completing the square. Solution: y = −(x² + 12x) − 9 = −(x² + 12x + 36) + 27 = −(x + 6)² + 27.

nodes.title: Example 10: Determine the Vertex and Axis of Symmetry

metadata.rawText: PDF page 37. Prompt: Consider y = 3x² − 12x + 5. Part A: Write the function in vertex form. Part B: Find the axis of symmetry. Part C: Find the vertex and state whether the vertex is a maximum or minimum. Demonstrated capability: Use vertex form to determine the axis of symmetry, vertex, and minimum value. Solution: y = 3(x − 2)² − 7; axis x = 2; vertex (2, −7); minimum.

nodes.title: Example 11: Model with a Quadratic Function

metadata.rawText: PDF page 38. Prompt: FIREWORKS If a firework is launched 1 foot off the ground at a velocity of 128 feet per second, write a function for the situation. Then find and interpret the axis of symmetry and vertex. Demonstrated capability: Model a projectile with a quadratic function and interpret its vertex and axis of symmetry. Solution: h(t) = −16t² + 128t + 1 = −16(t − 4)² + 257; axis t = 4; vertex (4, 257), maximum.

nodes.title: Example 1: Real Roots, c Is Positive

metadata.rawText: Prompt: At the World Championship Punkin Chunkin contest in Bridgeville, Delaware, pumpkins are launched hundreds of yards. The path of a pumpkin can be modeled by h = -4.9t^2 + 11.7t + 42, where h is the height and t is the number of seconds after launch. Part A Use the Quadratic Formula to solve 0 = -4.9t^2 + 11.7t + 42. Part B Interpret the roots. Solution: The approximate solutions are 4.4 seconds and -2.0 seconds. The negative root does not make sense in this context because the pumpkin launches at 0 seconds. The pumpkin lands after 4.4 seconds. Demonstrated capability: Use the Quadratic Formula to solve a quadratic equation and interpret roots in context.

nodes.title: Example 2: Real Roots, c Is Negative

metadata.rawText: Prompt: Solve x^2 + 4x - 17 = 0 by using the Quadratic Formula. Solution: x = -2 ± sqrt(21). Demonstrated capability: Use the Quadratic Formula to solve a quadratic equation with two real irrational roots.

nodes.title: Example 3: Complex Roots

metadata.rawText: Prompt: Solve 5x^2 + 8x + 11 = 0 by using the Quadratic Formula. Solution: x = (-4 ± i sqrt(39))/5. Demonstrated capability: Use the Quadratic Formula to solve a quadratic equation with two complex roots.

nodes.title: Example 4: The Discriminant, Real Roots

metadata.rawText: Prompt: Examine 2x^2 - 10x + 7 = 0. Part A Find the value of the discriminant for 2x^2 - 10x + 7 = 0. Part B Describe the number and type of roots for the equation. Solution: The discriminant is 44. There are two real irrational roots. Demonstrated capability: Use the discriminant to find its value and determine that the equation has two real irrational roots.

nodes.title: Example 5: The Discriminant, Complex Roots

metadata.rawText: Prompt: Examine -5x^2 + 10x - 15 = 0. Part A Find the value of the discriminant for -5x^2 + 10x - 15 = 0. Part B Describe the number and type of roots for the equation. Solution: The discriminant is -200. There are two complex roots. Demonstrated capability: Use the discriminant to find its value and determine that the equation has two complex roots.

nodes.title: Example 1: Graph a Quadratic Inequality (< or ≤)

metadata.demonstratedCapability: Graph the related quadratic function. Use a solid boundary for a less-than-or-equal-to inequality. Test (0,0). Shade the region that contains the test point.
metadata.solutionText: The boundary is y = x^2 - 2x + 8. The point (0,0) satisfies 0 <= 8, so shade the region that contains (0,0).
metadata.rawText: PDF page 51, Example 1 — Graph a Quadratic Inequality (< or ≤): Graph y ≤ x^2 - 2x + 8.

nodes.title: Example 2: Graph a Quadratic Inequality (> or ≥)

metadata.demonstratedCapability: Graph the related quadratic function. Use a dashed boundary for a greater-than inequality. Since (0,0) lies on the boundary, test (1,0). Shade the opposite region when the test point fails.
metadata.solutionText: The boundary is y = -5x^2 + 10x. The point (0,0) lies on the boundary, so test (1,0). The statement 0 > 5 is false, so shade the region that does not contain (1,0).
metadata.rawText: PDF page 52, Example 2 — Graph a Quadratic Inequality (> or ≥): Graph y > -5x^2 + 10x.

nodes.title: Example 3: Solve a Quadratic Inequality (< or ≤) by Graphing

metadata.demonstratedCapability: Graph the related equation. Find the zeros. Identify where the graph is below the x-axis. State the open interval because the inequality is strict.
metadata.solutionText: The zeros are x = -3 and x = 2 because x^2 + x - 6 = (x - 2)(x + 3). The graph is below the x-axis on (-3, 2).
metadata.rawText: PDF page 53, Example 3 — Solve x^2 + x - 6 < 0 by graphing.

nodes.title: Example 4: Solve a Quadratic Inequality (> or ≥) by Graphing

metadata.demonstratedCapability: Graph the related equation. Find the zeros. Identify where the graph is on or above the x-axis. Include the zeros because the inequality is inclusive.
metadata.solutionText: The zeros are x = -1 and x = 4 because x^2 - 3x - 4 = (x - 4)(x + 1). The graph is on or above the x-axis on (-∞, -1] U [4, ∞).
metadata.rawText: PDF page 53, Example 4 — Solve x^2 - 3x - 4 ≥ 0 by graphing.

nodes.title: Example 5: Solve a Quadratic Inequality Algebraically

metadata.authoredPrompt: GARDENING Marcus is planning a garden. He has enough soil to cover 104 square feet, and wants the dimensions of the garden to be at least 5 feet by 10 feet. If he wants to increase the length and width by the same number of feet, by what value can he increase the dimensions of the garden without needing to buy more soil? Create a quadratic inequality and solve it algebraically.
metadata.demonstratedCapability: Model the garden area with a quadratic inequality. Solve the related quadratic equation. Use the practical domain to select the increase that does not exceed the soil limit.
metadata.solutionText: The area inequality is (x + 10)(x + 5) <= 104. The related equation has roots x = -18 and x = 3. The practical solution is [0, 3], so Marcus can increase each dimension by up to 3 feet.
metadata.rawText: PDF page 54, Example 5 — Solve a Quadratic Inequality Algebraically.
